example.about.citing.p1: Cloudflare Radar data is increasingly referenced in academic papers, formal reports, and policy documents. We encourage proper attribution when using Radar data. Use the generator below to create a citation in your preferred format, or use the cite <icon /> button on individual widgets throughout the site.
example.about.citing.title: Citing Radar
example.about.cloudflare.p1: Cloudflare, Inc. <link1>www.cloudflare.com</link1> / <link2>@cloudflare</link2> is on a mission to help build a better Internet. Cloudflare's suite of products protects and accelerates any Internet application online without adding hardware, installing software, or changing a line of code. Internet properties powered by Cloudflare have all web traffic routed through its intelligent global network, which gets smarter with every request. As a result, they see significant improvement in performance and a decrease in spam and other attacks. Cloudflare was named to Entrepreneur Magazine's Top Company Cultures 2018 list and ranked among the World's Most Innovative Companies by Fast Company in 2019.
example.about.cloudflare.p2: Headquartered in San Francisco, CA, Cloudflare has offices in Austin, TX, Champaign, IL, New York, NY, San Jose, CA, Seattle, WA, Washington, D.C., Toronto, Dubai, Lisbon, London, Munich, Paris, Beijing, Singapore, Sydney, and Tokyo.
example.about.cloudflare.title: About Cloudflare
example.about.license.li1: Embeddable and downloadable graphs and images on radar.cloudflare.com are available for public use under the <link1>CC BY 4.0</link1> license.
example.about.license.li2: Data available via <link1>Radar API</link1> endpoints or direct download from radar.cloudflare.com is made available under the <link2>CC BY-NC 4.0</link2> license.
example.about.license.li3: You are free to use limited excerpts from <link1>Cloudflare Radar Reports</link1> provided you give proper attribution to Cloudflare by including in your attribution notice the report's title, a link to the report, and identify Cloudflare as the source.
example.about.license.p1: Unless otherwise indicated, content accessible from radar.cloudflare.com is made available as follows:
example.about.license.p2: Rights in the trademarks and service marks of Cloudflare, as well as the look and feel of radar.cloudflare.com, are not licensed under the terms mentioned above. Please see our <link1>Trademark Guidelines</link1> for more information.
example.about.license.p3: If you have questions on how to cite or display the data above, or would like to request an exception, please reach out to <email>{{email}}</email>.
example.about.license.title: Licensing Policies
example.about.localization.p1: We have carefully localized Radar into each language using industry and Cloudflare terminology. If you find any issues or want to drop us a line with a suggestion, please let us know at <link1>radar_localization@cloudflare.com</link1>
example.about.localization.title: Localization
example.about.maps.p1: Cloudflare Radar uses map data from <link1>Natural Earth</link1>. The maps reflect Natural Earth's <link2>disputed boundaries policy</link2> with the US worldview enabled for administrative geographies.
example.about.maps.title: Maps
example.about.radar.p1: Cloudflare Radar is a hub that showcases global Internet traffic, attack, and technology trends and insights. Cloudflare Radar is powered by data from Cloudflare's global network, as well as aggregated and anonymized data from Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 public DNS Resolver.
example.about.radar.p2: In some cases Cloudflare Radar uses data from <link1>PeeringDB</link1>  (interconnection meta-information) and <link2>APNIC</link2> (visible ASNs customer population measurements).
example.about.radar.p3: With Radar, you can access trends and insights, like the adoption of new technologies, browsers or operating systems. Radar also keeps up to date with relevant events around the world to provide information on Internet activity patterns.
example.about.radar.title: Cloudflare Radar
example.about.regional-data.p1: Cloudflare Radar uses <link1>"first-order administrative divisions"</link1> data from <link2>GeoNames</link2>. For more information about geographical data provided by GeoNames, please refer to their <link3>About</link3> page.
example.about.regional-data.title: Regional Data
example.about.routing.li1: RIPEstat, the “one-stop shop” for all available information about Internet number resources. RIPEstat uses individual widgets to display routing and other information.
example.about.routing.li2: RIS Live, a real time BGP streaming API allowing server-side filtering of BGP messages by prefix or autonomous system.
example.about.routing.li3: RIS Raw Data, available for each route collector, with state dumps and batches of updates made available periodically.
example.about.routing.li4: RISwhois, that searches the latest RIS data for details of an IP address using a plaintext “whois”-style interface. It is useful when querying RIS data using scripts.
example.about.routing.p1: The Routing section on Cloudflare Radar uses <link1>RIPE RIS</link1> data from RIPE NCC.
example.about.routing.p2: The RIPE Routing Information Service (RIS) is a RIPE NCC service. With the help of network operators all over the world, RIS employs a globally distributed set of Remote Route Collectors (RRCs), typically located at Internet Exchange Points, to collect and store Internet routing data. Volunteers peer with the RRCs using the BGP protocol and RIS stores the update and withdraw messages. RIS data can be accessed via:
example.about.routing.p3: The Routing section on Cloudflare Radar uses University of Oregon's <link1>RouteViews</link1> data, which is licensed under <link2>CC BY 4.0</link2>

example.mrt-explorer.info-block:
Collectors like RIPE RIS and RouteViews publish MRT dump files containing BGP announcements, withdrawals, and route attributes.

This tool parses MRT files entirely in the browser (nothing gets uploaded). Supports gzip and bzip2 compression.
Paste a URL, drag, browse or try a sample file to explore BGP messages, AS paths, community attributes and more.
example.mrt-explorer.info.atomic:
ATOMIC_AGGREGATE is a BGP path attribute indicating this route has been summarized from multiple more-specific prefixes. The original AS path details are no longer available.

Click to learn more...
example.mrt-explorer.info.communities:
BGP community attributes attached to the route, used for routing policy signaling.

Click to learn more...
example.mrt-explorer.info.local-pref:
Local Preference is a BGP path attribute used within an autonomous system to indicate the preferred path for outbound traffic. Higher values are more preferred.

Click to learn more...
example.mrt-explorer.info.med:
Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) is a BGP attribute used to suggest to neighboring autonomous systems the preferred entry point when multiple paths exist.

Click to learn more...
example.mrt-explorer.info.otc:
Only to Customer is a BGP attribute that prevents route leaks by restricting propagation to customer ASes.

Click to learn more...
example.mrt-explorer.status.nodata: The file was parsed but no valid records were found.

example.post-quantum.host-test.description: Check if a host supports post-quantum TLS key exchange
example.post-quantum.host-test.footer: This tool initiates a TLS handshake with the specified host and examines the key exchange algorithm negotiated during the connection. We check if the server supports post-quantum key exchange methods like X25519MLKEM768, a hybrid algorithm combining classical X25519 with the ML-KEM post-quantum algorithm. The test connects to port 443 by default (the standard HTTPS port), but you can specify a different port for services running TLS on non-standard ports, such as port 853 for DNS over TLS or port 8443 for alternative HTTPS.
example.post-quantum.host-test.issues.hrr-failur: The server sent a HelloRetryRequest during the TLS 1.3 handshake but failed to complete it afterward. This is often caused by non-compliant TLS 1.3 implementations that do not properly handle the HelloRetryRequest mechanism.

Verify that the server's TLS implementation fully supports the HelloRetryRequest mechanism as defined in <rfc8446>RFC 8446</rfc8446>. This issue is common with shared hosting providers or outdated TLS libraries.
example.post-quantum.host-test.issues.split-clie: The connection to the server failed when using a TLS ClientHello message fragmented due to a large post-quantum key share, but succeeded with classical (non-PQ) handshakes. This is typically caused by middleboxes (firewalls, load balancers, or DPI devices) that cannot reassemble split TLS ClientHello messages.
Check for middleboxes or firewalls between clients and the server that may be interfering with large TLS handshakes. See <pqDocs>Cloudflare's post-quantum documentation</pqDocs> for more details.
example.post-quantum.host-test.issues.title: TLS issues · {{n}} found
example.post-quantum.host-test.issues.unknown-ke: The server cannot handle an unknown key exchange algorithm in the ClientHello key share extension and fails instead of falling back gracefully. A compliant TLS 1.3 server should respond with a HelloRetryRequest to negotiate a supported algorithm.
Update the server's TLS implementation to handle unsupported key share groups by issuing a HelloRetryRequest, as specified in <rfc8446Section>RFC 8446 §4.1.4</rfc8446Section>.

example.speedtest.disclaimer.dataUsage: A speed test can consume up to 200MB of data.
example.speedtest.disclaimer.fullPolicy:
When you use Speed Test, Cloudflare receives the IP address you use to connect to Cloudflare’s Speed Test service. Cloudflare uses your IP address to estimate your geolocation (at the country and city levels) and to identify the Autonomous System Number (ASN) associated with your IP address.

Cloudflare shares anonymized measurement information (e.g., the estimated geolocation, ASN associated with your Speed Test, etc.) with our measurement partners as part of Cloudflare's contribution to a shared Internet performance database. We do not share your IP address with our measurement partners.

As a part of this Speed Test, Cloudflare receives the following information:

- Your IP address;
- An estimate of your location (Country, City);
- The Autonomous System Number of your ISP (ASN).

Cloudflare truncates your IP address that it receives as part of your use of the Speed Test to /24 and /48 for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, respectively.

Top-level domains ranked by their DNS Magnitude — a metric estimating the popularity of a TLD based on the number of unique networks querying Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1 resolver.

The magnitude value ranges from 0 to 10, with higher values (closer to 10) indicating that the TLD is queried by a broader range of clients, reflecting greater global visibility and broader usage across the Internet.

example.tld.information.type.country-code.info: Country code top-level domains (ccTLDs) are country-specific top-level domains that are reserved for use in a specific country, sovereign state, or dependent territory.
Generic restricted top-level domains (grTLDs) are generic top-level domains (gTLDs) that have restrictions on who can register them, requiring applicants to meet specific criteria related to their profession or purpose.
example.tld.information.type.generic.info: Generic top-level domains (gTLDs) are top-level domains that are not reserved for specific purposes and are available for registration by anyone.
example.tld.information.type.infrastructure.info: The infrastructure top-level domain (iTLD) is a single, specialized top-level domain, .arpa (Address and Routing Parameter Area), reserved for operational internet infrastructure purposes and not for public registration or general website use.
example.tld.information.type.sponsored.info: Sponsored top-level domains (sTLDs) are top-level domains that represent a specific community, setting and enforcing rules for its use.

example.arg.aggInterval.info: Aggregation interval results should be returned in (for example, in 15 minutes or 1 hour intervals). Refer to [Aggregation intervals](https://developers.cloudflare.com/radar/concepts/aggregation-intervals/)
example.arg.arc.info: Filters results by ARC (Authenticated Received Chain) validation
example.arg.asn.info: Comma-separated list of Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs). Prefix with `-` to exclude ASNs from results. For example, `-174, 3356` excludes results from AS174, but includes results from AS3356
example.arg.asn2.info: AS relationship of ASN2 with respect to the given ASN
example.arg.botClass.info: Filters results by bot class. Refer to [Bot classes](https://developers.cloudflare.com/radar/concepts/bot-classes/)
example.arg.bucketSize.info: Width for every bucket in the histogram
example.arg.checkResult.info: Filters results by leaked credential check result
example.arg.compromised.info: Filters results by compromised credential status
example.arg.contentType.info: Filters results by content type category (based on MIME type)
example.arg.continent.info: Comma-separated list of continents (alpha-2 continent codes). Prefix with `-` to exclude continents from results. For example, `-EU,NA` excludes results from EU, but includes results from NA
example.arg.date.info: Array of dates to filter the ranking
example.arg.dateRange.info: Filters results by the specified date range. For example, use `7d` and `7dcontrol` to compare this week with the previous week. Use this parameter or set specific start and end dates (`dateStart` and `dateEnd` parameters)
example.arg.debug.info: Includes the performed GraphQL query in the response (staging only)
example.arg.direction.info: Together with the `location` parameter, will apply the filter to origin or target location
example.arg.dkim.info: Filters results by DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) validation status
example.arg.dmarc.info: Filters results by DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) validation status
example.arg.encrypted.info: Filters results by encryption status (encrypted vs. not-encrypted)
example.arg.eventId.info: The unique identifier of a event
example.arg.exclude.info: Search types to be excluded from results
example.arg.format.info: Format in which results will be returned
example.arg.hasIps.info: Whether the certificates are bound to specific IP addresses
example.arg.hasWildcards.info: Whether the certificates contain wildcard domains
example.arg.hijackerAsn.info: The potential hijacker AS of a BGP hijack event
example.arg.httpProtocol.info: Filters results by HTTP protocol (HTTP vs. HTTPS)
example.arg.include.info: Search types to be included in results
example.arg.includeTopLocations.info: Includes top locations in the response
example.arg.industry.info: A focused segment within a vertical.
example.arg.interpolation.info: Enables interpolation for all series (using the average)
example.arg.involvedAsn.info: The potential hijacker or victim AS of a BGP hijack event
example.arg.involvedCountry.info: The country code of the potential hijacker or victim AS of a BGP hijack event
example.arg.ipVersion.info: Filters results by IP version (Ipv4 vs. IPv6)
example.arg.leakAsn.info: The leaking AS of a route leak event
example.arg.limit.info: Limits the number of objects returned in the response
example.arg.limitDirection.info: Array of attack origin/target location attack limits. Together with `limitPerLocation`, limits how many objects will be fetched per origin/target location
example.arg.limitPerGroup.info: Limits the number of objects per group to the top items within the specified time range. If there are more items than the limit, the response will include the count of items, with any remaining items grouped together under an "other" category
example.arg.limitPerLocation.info: Limits the number of attacks per origin/target (refer to `limitDirection` parameter) location
example.arg.location.info: Comma-separated list of locations (alpha-2 codes). Prefix with `-` to exclude locations from results. For example, `-US,PT` excludes results from the US, but includes results from PT
example.arg.longestPrefixMatch.info: Return only results with the longest prefix match for the given prefix. For example, specify a /32 prefix to lookup the origin ASN for an IPv4 address
example.arg.magnitude.info: Attack magnitude can be defined by total requests mitigated or by total zones attacked
example.arg.maxConfidence.info: The maximum confidence score to filter events (1-4 low, 5-7 mid, 8+ high)
example.arg.metric.info: Defines which metric to return (bandwidth, latency, or DNS response time)
example.arg.minConfidence.info: The minimum confidence score to filter events (1-4 low, 5-7 mid, 8+ high)
example.arg.name.info: Array of names used to label the series in the response
example.arg.offset.info: Skips the specified number of objects before fetching the results
example.arg.orderBy.info: Metric to order the results by
example.arg.origin.info: Lookup MOASes originated by the given ASN
example.arg.pattern.info: Filters results by pattern ("FULLY" vs. "PARTIALLY"). A user agent is classified as "fully allowed" or "fully disallowed" if the directive value is *. Otherwise, if the user agent is only allowed or disallowed to crawl specific paths, it is classified as "partially allowed" or "partially disallowed."
example.arg.product.info: Array of network traffic product types to filters results by
example.arg.protocol.info: Filters results by DNS transport protocol
example.arg.query.info: Search for locations, autonomous systems and reports
example.arg.queryType.info: Filters results by DNS query type
example.arg.responseCode.info: Filters results by DNS response code
example.arg.rpkiStatus.info: Return only results with matching rpki status: valid, invalid or unknown
example.arg.serviceCategory.info: Filters results by Internet service category
example.arg.sortBy.info: Sorts results by the specified field
example.arg.spf.info: Filters results by SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation status
example.arg.tld.info: Filters results by country code top-level domain (ccTLD)
example.arg.uniqueEntries.info: Whether filter out duplicate certificates and pre-certificates.
example.arg.userAgentCategory.info: Filters results by user agent category
example.arg.vertical.info: Verticals include pre-defined collections of related industries.
example.arg.victimAsn.info: The potential victim AS of a BGP hijack event
